\begin{document}

\begin{abstract}
For every non-Gelfand Sabidussi pair $(G,H)$ in the catalogue of cubic
arc-transitive graphs, we compute all irreducible representations of the
Hecke algebra $\HH(G,H) = \operatorname{End}_G \C[G/H]$ explicitly:
one-dimensional character tables for the Gelfand summands, and exact
matrix entries (over cyclotomic fields) for every irreducible block of
dimension $\ge 2$.  The Wedderburn decomposition, a minimal generating
set with complete relations, and the expansion of every orbital generator
as a word in the block generators are recorded for each graph.
All data was computed exactly over cyclotomic fields by isotypic
restriction in GAP and independently verified.
\end{abstract}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}
%% ===================================================================

\subsection{Symmetric graphs and Sabidussi's construction}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, colback=black!5, colframe=black!5,
  boxrule=0pt, sharp corners]
A graph $\Gamma$ is \emph{symmetric} (or \emph{arc-transitive}) if its
automorphism group $G = \operatorname{Aut}(\Gamma)$ acts transitively on
the set of arcs (ordered pairs of adjacent vertices).  This is a
stronger condition than vertex-transitivity: it requires that the local
neighbourhood of every vertex ``looks the same,'' not just that every
vertex is equivalent.

The fundamental observation, due to Sabidussi~\cite{sabidussi}, is that
every symmetric graph arises as a \emph{coset graph}.  Given a group
$G$, a subgroup $H \le G$, and an element $a \in G$ with
$a \notin H$ and $a^2 \in H$, the \textbf{Sabidussi graph}
$\operatorname{Sab}(G, H, HaH)$ is the graph with:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Vertices:} the right cosets $G/H = \{Hg : g \in G\}$,
\item \textbf{Edges:} $\{Hx, Hy\}$ whenever $xy^{-1} \in HaH$.
\end{itemize}
Every symmetric graph is isomorphic to $\operatorname{Sab}(G, H, HaH)$
for some triple $(G, H, a)$, and conversely every such triple produces a
symmetric graph (Lorimer's theorem; see~\cite{langer}).
\end{tcolorbox}

The cubic arc-transitive graphs are those symmetric graphs in which every
vertex has exactly three neighbours.  The condition $a^2 \in H$ ensures
that each double coset $HaH$ defines an undirected adjacency relation,
and the valency equals $|H|/|H \cap a^{-1}Ha|$.  For cubic graphs this
is~$3$, which constrains $[H : H \cap a^{-1}Ha] = 3$: the stabilizer
$H$ is ``almost normal'' with respect to conjugation by $a$.

\subsection{Orbitals and double cosets}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, colback=yellow!10, colframe=yellow!10,
  boxrule=0pt, sharp corners]
Once $\Gamma = \operatorname{Sab}(G, H, HaH)$ is fixed, the group $G$
acts on the vertex set $G/H$ and hence on pairs of vertices
$(G/H) \times (G/H)$.  The orbits of this action are called
\textbf{orbitals}, and they are in natural bijection with the double
cosets of $H$ in $G$:
\[
  \{\text{orbitals of } (G, G/H)\}
  \;\longleftrightarrow\;
  \{H \backslash G / H\}
  \;=\; \{HgH : g \in G\}.
\]
The trivial orbital (the diagonal) corresponds to the double coset
$H \cdot 1 \cdot H = H$.  The adjacency relation of $\Gamma$
corresponds to $HaH$.  The remaining double cosets encode higher-order
structural relations: distance-2 neighbours, distance-3 neighbours, and
(when the graph is not distance-transitive) finer orbital splittings
within each distance class.

Each orbital has a \textbf{valency} $k_i = |HgH|/|H|$: the number of
vertices in the $i$-th suborbit of the point stabilizer.  The total
number of orbitals is the \textbf{rank} $r$ of the pair $(G, H)$, and
$\sum_i k_i = |G/H|$.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{The Hecke algebra}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=black!5, colframe=black!5, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\begin{definition}[Hecke algebra]\label{def:hecke}
Let $G$ be a finite group and $H \le G$.  The \textbf{Hecke algebra}
of the pair $(G,H)$ is the endomorphism algebra of the permutation
representation:
\[
  \HH(G,H) \;=\; \operatorname{End}_G \C[G/H].
\]
Equivalently, $\HH(G,H)$ is the algebra of $G$-invariant operators on
the vector space with basis $G/H$, or the convolution algebra of
$H$-bi-invariant functions on $G$.
\end{definition}
\end{tcolorbox}

A natural basis for $\HH(G,H)$ is the set of \emph{orbital matrices}
$T_1 = I, T_2, \ldots, T_r$: the adjacency matrices of the $r$ orbitals,
or equivalently the characteristic functions of the double cosets $HgH$.
These satisfy the product rule
\[
  T_i \cdot T_j = \sum_{k=1}^{r} p_{ij}^k \, T_k,
\]
where $p_{ij}^k$ are the \emph{intersection numbers}, determined by the
combinatorics of the coset geometry.

By the Wedderburn--Artin theorem and Schur's double-centralizer duality,
the Hecke algebra decomposes as
\[
  \HH(G,H) \;\cong\; \bigoplus_{\chi} M_{m_\chi}(\C),
  \qquad m_\chi = \langle \operatorname{Ind}_H^G \mathbf{1},\, \chi \rangle,
\]
where the sum runs over those irreducible characters $\chi$ of $G$ that
appear in $\C[G/H]$, and $m_\chi$ is the multiplicity.  Each summand
$M_{m_\chi}(\C)$ is a full matrix algebra of dimension $m_\chi^2$, and
the rank satisfies $r = \sum_\chi m_\chi^2$.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, colback=yellow!10, colframe=yellow!10,
  boxrule=0pt, sharp corners]
The pair $(G,H)$ is a \textbf{Gelfand pair} when every $m_\chi \le 1$,
i.e.\ when $\HH$ is commutative.  In that case every irreducible
representation is one-dimensional --- a \emph{spherical function}
$\omega_\chi \colon T_i \mapsto \lambda_i \in \C$ --- and the structure
reduces to the classical theory of association schemes and
distance-regular graphs.

The non-Gelfand pairs are more interesting: they contain irreducible
representations of dimension $m \ge 2$, yielding $m \times m$ matrix
blocks whose entries live in cyclotomic number fields.  These are the
primary objects of this catalog.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{From the thesis to this catalog}

In \emph{Symmetric Graphs and their Quotients}~\cite{langer}, the
relationship between a symmetric graph $\Gamma$ and its quotients was
studied through Sabidussi's construction: a quotient $\Sigma$ of
$\Gamma = \operatorname{Sab}(G, H, HaH)$ is itself a Sabidussi graph
$\operatorname{Sab}(G, K, KaK)$ for some $H < K < G$ (Lorimer's
theorem).  The passage from $\Gamma$ to $\Sigma$ collapses orbits of
$K$; the passage from $\HH(G,H)$ to $\HH(G,K)$ collapses double
cosets.

This catalog completes a different layer of the same picture: instead
of passing to quotients (which changes $H$), we fix $(G,H)$ and compute
the \emph{full representation theory} of $\HH(G,H)$.  The irreducible
representations of the Hecke algebra decompose the permutation module
$\C[G/H]$ into its finest $G$-invariant pieces, revealing the
algebraic structure that governs how the graph's symmetry interacts
with its combinatorics.

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=blue!5, colframe=blue!5, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\begin{observation}[The three levels of structure]\label{obs:levels}
For a Sabidussi graph $\Gamma = \operatorname{Sab}(G, H, HaH)$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Quotients} (thesis): vary $K$ with $H < K < G$;
  collapse orbits; passage from fine graph to coarser graph.
\item \textbf{Orbitals} (this catalog): fix $(G,H)$; study all double
  cosets $H \backslash G / H$; the rank-$r$ Hecke algebra.
\item \textbf{Representations} (this catalog): decompose $\HH$ into
  irreducible blocks; extract exact matrices over cyclotomic fields.
\end{enumerate}
\end{observation}
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Notation}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=black!5, colframe=black!5, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
Throughout, $T_1 = I, T_2, \ldots, T_r$ is the orbital basis of $\HH$,
sorted by suborbit length $k_i$ (ties ordered by the orbit enumeration
of the generating GAP session; the numbering is fixed unambiguously by
the explicit matrices below).

Recurring algebraic constants:
\medskip

\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.4}
\begin{tabular}{llll}
  \toprule
  Symbol & Value & Satisfies & Field \\
  \midrule
  $\alpha$ & $\frac{-1+\sqrt{-7}}{2}$
    & $\alpha^2+\alpha+2=0$, $\alpha\bar\alpha=2$
    & $\Q(\sqrt{-7})$ \\
  $\eta_0, \eta_1$ & $\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{13}}{2}$
    & $\eta^2+\eta-3=0$, $\eta_0\eta_1=-3$
    & $\Q(\sqrt{13})$ \\
  $c_k$ & $\zeta_7^k + \zeta_7^{-k}$
    & $c_1+c_2+c_3=-1$
    & $\Q(\zeta_7)^+$ \\
  $\omega$ & $e^{2\pi i/3}$
    & $\omega^2+\omega+1=0$
    & $\Q(\zeta_3)$ \\
  \bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\medskip

$\eta_a = \sum_{s \in H_p} \zeta_p^{as}$ denotes the sextic Gauss
period of $\Q(\zeta_p)$ over the index-$6$ subgroup
$H_p \le (\Z/p)^\times$.
\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Dodecahedron: $\bigl(\mathrm{PSL}(2,5),\,C_3\bigr)$}
%% ===================================================================

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=black!5, colframe=black!5, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\textbf{Graph.} The dodecahedron on $20 = |\mathrm{PSL}(2,5)|/3$
vertices.  Under the full group $C_2 \times A_5$ the pair is Gelfand;
the representation theory below belongs to the refined pair
$G = \mathrm{PSL}(2,5) \cong A_5$, $H = C_3$.

\medskip
\textbf{Algebra.} Rank $8$,
$\HH \cong \C^4 \oplus M_2(\C)$.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=yellow!10, colframe=yellow!10, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\textbf{Highlights.} The valency-3 generator satisfies $B^2 + B + 3I = 0$
($\det B = 3 = {}$valency); the golden $\pm\sqrt{5}$ of the dodecahedron
spectrum lives entirely in the 1-dimensional characters.  The ``why-$N$''
constant of this 20-point Meinhold miniature is $4$:
$(\rho(T_6) - I)^2 = 4I$.
\end{tcolorbox}

\input{catalog-data/dodeca}

\section{F26A: $\bigl(C_{13}{:}C_6,\,C_3\bigr)$}
%% ===================================================================

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=black!5, colframe=black!5, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\textbf{Graph.} F26A, the unique cubic arc-transitive graph on 26
vertices; $G = C_{13}{:}C_6$ ($|G| = 78$) is \emph{sharply}
arc-transitive, $H = C_3$.

\medskip
\textbf{Algebra.} Rank $10$,
$\HH \cong \C^2 \oplus M_2(\C) \oplus M_2(\C)$, the two blocks Galois
conjugate over $\Q(\sqrt{13})$ (the substitution
$\sqrt{13} \mapsto -\sqrt{13}$ maps Block~1 to Block~2).
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=yellow!10, colframe=yellow!10, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\textbf{Highlights.} With
$\eta_0, \eta_1 = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{13}}{2}$ the sextic Gauss periods
of $\Q(\zeta_{13})$, the traceless generators satisfy
\[
  B^2 = \frac{5-\sqrt{13}}{2}\,I \quad(\text{Block 1}),\qquad
  B^2 = \frac{5+\sqrt{13}}{2}\,I \quad(\text{Block 2}),\qquad
  N_+ N_- = 3 = \text{valency},
\]
and $\frac{5 \mp \sqrt{13}}{2} = 3 + \eta$: \emph{valency plus a Gauss
period} (see the Remark after CR(31)).
\end{tcolorbox}

\input{catalog-data/f26a}

\section{CR(19): $\bigl(C_{19}{:}C_6,\,C_3\bigr)$}
%% ===================================================================

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=black!5, colframe=black!5, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\textbf{Graph.} The 38-vertex cubic arc-transitive Frobenius graph;
$G = C_{19}{:}C_6$ ($|G| = 114$), $H = C_3$.  Here
$H_{19} = \langle 8 \rangle = \{1,7,8,11,12,18\} \le (\Z/19)^\times$
and the three sextic periods are $\eta_1, \eta_2, \eta_4$ (indexed by
coset representatives $1,2,4$), satisfying $\eta_1 + \eta_2 + \eta_4 = -1$;
entries below are written in the basis $\{1, \eta_a, \eta_b\}$ that gives
the sparsest expression.

\medskip
\textbf{Algebra.} Rank $14$,
$\HH \cong \C^2 \oplus M_2(\C)^{\oplus 3}$.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=yellow!10, colframe=yellow!10, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\textbf{Highlights.} The three blocks are permuted cyclically by the
Galois action $a \mapsto 2a$ on period indices; in each, the traceless
valency-3 orbital squares to $(3 + \eta)I$.
\end{tcolorbox}

\input{catalog-data/cr19}

\section{CR(31): $\bigl(C_{31}{:}C_6,\,C_3\bigr)$}
%% ===================================================================

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=black!5, colframe=black!5, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
{\sloppy
\textbf{Graph.} The 62-vertex sibling; $G = C_{31}{:}C_6$ ($|G| = 186$),
$H = C_3$.  Here
$H_{31} = \langle 26 \rangle = \{1,5,6,25,26,30\}$, and there are five
sextic periods $\eta_1, \eta_2, \eta_3, \eta_4, \eta_8$ (coset
representatives $1,2,3,4,8$), summing to $-1$.\par}

\medskip
\textbf{Algebra.} Rank $22$,
$\HH \cong \C^2 \oplus M_2(\C)^{\oplus 5}$.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=yellow!10, colframe=yellow!10, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\textbf{Highlights.} Five Galois-conjugate blocks, cycled by
$a \mapsto 2a$; same $(3 + \eta)$-law as CR(19).
\end{tcolorbox}

\input{catalog-data/cr31}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=blue!5, colframe=blue!5, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\begin{remark}[A uniform law for the Frobenius family]
In all three graphs F26A, CR(19), CR(31) the traceless valency-3
generator satisfies
\[
  T^2 = (3 + \eta)\,I
\]
where $3$ is the valency and $\eta$ is a sextic Gauss period of
$\Q(\zeta_p)$.  For $p = 13$ this is
$3 + \frac{-1 \mp \sqrt{13}}{2} = \frac{5 \mp \sqrt{13}}{2}$, recovering
the F26A relation.  The ``why-$N$'' constant of the whole family is
\emph{valency plus a Gauss period}.
\end{remark}
\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Klein graph F056A: $\bigl(\mathrm{PSL}(2,7),\,C_3\bigr)$}
%% ===================================================================

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=black!5, colframe=black!5, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\textbf{Graph.} F056A, the 56-vertex cubic arc-transitive graph of
girth 6 on the cosets $\mathrm{PSL}(2,7)/C_3$;
$G = \mathrm{PSL}(2,7)$ ($|G| = 168$), $H = C_3$.

\medskip
\textbf{Algebra.} Rank $20$,
$\HH \cong \C^3 \oplus M_2(\C) \oplus M_3(\C) \oplus M_2(\C)$
(blocks on $\chi_4, \chi_5, \chi_6$ of degrees $6, 7, 8$).
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=yellow!10, colframe=yellow!10, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\textbf{Highlights.} Block~1 is generated by the $\alpha$-diagonal
orbital ($A^2 + A + 2I = 0$; $2 = \alpha\bar\alpha$ is the prime that
splits in $\Q(\sqrt{-7})$).  Block~2, the integral $M_3$, carries the
irreducible characteristic polynomial $x^3 + x - 6$ --- the first
genuinely cubic eigenvalue in the catalogue, echoed by
$\mathrm{PSL}(2,13)$'s $x^3 + x - 26$ below.  In Block~3 the order-3
matrix
$\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1/2 & 1 \\ -7/4 & -3/2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$
appears as $\rho(T_{10})$ --- see the Remark after the Klein $\{7,3\}$
section.
\end{tcolorbox}

\input{catalog-data/f056a}

\section{Klein $\{3,7\}$ graph: $\bigl(\mathrm{PGL}(2,7),\,D_7\bigr)$}
%% ===================================================================

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=black!5, colframe=black!5, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\textbf{Graph.} The 1-skeleton of the $\{3,7\}$ tiling of the Klein
quartic: 24 vertices, valency 7 (the dual of the $\{7,3\}$ map).
$G = \operatorname{Aut}\Gamma \cong \mathrm{PGL}(2,7)$ ($|G| = 336$,
GAP-verified), with vertex stabilizer $H \cong D_7$ (dihedral of order
14).

\medskip
\textbf{Algebra.} Rank $6$,
$\HH \cong \C^2 \oplus M_2(\C)$.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=yellow!10, colframe=yellow!10, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\textbf{Highlights.} The stabilizer fixes three vertices, and the two
non-trivial valency-1 orbitals act as the $\omega$-diagonal pair
($A^2 + A + I = 0$, so $\rho(T_2)$ has order 3).  The symmetric
valency-7 orbital satisfies
\[
  B^2 = 7I
\]
--- the ``why-$N$'' constant equals the valency on the nose, the cleanest
instance in the catalogue --- and the chiral valency-7 pair is exactly
$\rho(T_5) = BA$, $\rho(T_6) = AB$, with $AB + BA = -B$.
\end{tcolorbox}

\input{catalog-data/klein37}

$\HH \cong \C^4 \oplus M_2(\C)^{\oplus 3} \oplus M_3(\C)^{\oplus 2}$.

characters (quadratic Gauss periods $\frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{13}}{2}$), a

\section{Meinhold-72: $\bigl(G_2(2),\,\mathrm{PSL}(3,2)\bigr)$}
%% ===================================================================

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=black!5, colframe=black!5, boxrule=0pt,
  sharp corners]
\textbf{Graph.} The Meinhold-72 orbital graph:
$G = G_2(2) = \mathrm{PSU}(3,3){:}2$ ($|G| = 12096$) acting on the $72$
cosets of $H = \mathrm{PSL}(3,2)$ (the $36 + 36$ chiral Fano
structures).

\medskip
\textbf{Algebra.} Rank $8$,
$\HH \cong \C^2 \oplus M_2(\C) \oplus \C^2$.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable, colback=yellow!10, colframe=yellow!10,
  boxrule=0pt, sharp corners]
\textbf{Highlights.} The block is generated by the mirror involution
$A = \rho(T_2)$ and the directed valency-7 orbital $B = \rho(T_3)$ with
\[
  A^2 = I, \qquad B^2 + 4B + 13I = 0\,;
\]
the roots $-2 \pm 3i$ of $x^2 + 4x + 13$ are Gaussian integers of norm
$13$.  Equivalently, the symmetric generator $\rho(T_4) = -4A - AB$
satisfies $\rho(T_4)^2 = 13I$ and $A\rho(T_4) + \rho(T_4)A = -4I$.

Why 13?{} $13 = 7 + 2 \cdot 3$: $NN^{\mathsf{T}} = 7I + 2A_{\mathrm{SRG}}$
for the $\mathrm{SRG}(36, 21, 12, 12)$ on the chiral Fano structures,
and $3 = \sqrt{k - \mu}$; the $-4$ is the $U_3(3)$-graph eigenvalue.
(Full account: \texttt{why13.pdf}.)
\end{tcolorbox}

\input{catalog-data/meinhold}
